analysis.one_liner: Sends monthly $2,000 checks to everyone during the COVID emergency, suspends rent, mortgage, and debt collection, and bans corporate stock buybacks.
analysis.headline: The bill, introduced in March 2020 with no cosponsors, was referred to six House committees and never received a vote or a hearing before Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: Representative Maxine Waters' bill responds to COVID-19 emergency with direct payments of $2,000 per adult and $1,000 per child monthly until unemployment recovers, sets up digital dollar accounts for people without bank accounts, suspends rent, mortgage, and debt payments, and bans corporations from buying back their own stock while receiving federal aid.
analysis.who_benefits: Every household receives monthly cash, renters and homeowners get eviction and foreclosure moratoriums, debt collectors are barred from suing or garnishing wages during the emergency, small businesses and community banks get credit lines, and state and local governments get access to a Federal Reserve municipal bond facility.

how_it_helps.text: Provides monthly $2,000 payments per adult ($1,000 per child) until unemployment drops within 2 percentage points of pre-pandemic levels, phased out for incomes above $75,000 [S2, S3]
Establishes digital dollar wallets through the Federal Reserve and postal service so people without bank accounts can receive stimulus money and avoid check-cashing fees [S3]
Suspends rent obligations for assisted housing tenants and bars eviction filings nationwide for the emergency duration, with no fees or credit-score penalties for nonpayment [S3]
Requires mortgage forbearance for any homeowner who requests it, with no fees or penalty interest accruing during forbearance [S3]
Prohibits debt collectors from suing, garnishing wages, repossessing cars, or shutting off utilities during the emergency, and blocks them from adding fees or penalty interest afterward [S3]
Bans stock buybacks temporarily and requires disclosure of supply-chain and pandemic risks to investors [S2, S3]
Authorizes $100 billion in emergency rental assistance, $15.5 billion for homeless services, and a $35 billion fund to prevent foreclosures [S3]

analysis.who_pays: The federal government pays for all the direct payments and assistance programs by authorizing the Federal Reserve to issue funds. Member banks must maintain no-fee digital dollar wallets and absorb operational costs, and mortgage servicers and landlords face payment suspensions (with some Federal Reserve credit facilities to offset losses). Corporations taking federal aid face stock buyback bans and warrant requirements.

drawbacks.text: Monthly universal payments for the duration of a multi-year emergency would cost trillions, far beyond the scale of the actual relief laws Congress passed that year [S2]

The Federal Reserve issuing digital wallets and becoming a retail bank for all citizens raises significant operational, privacy, and monetary-policy questions, and banks would be required to offer no-fee accounts regardless of profitability [S3]
Landlords, mortgage servicers, and creditors bear significant payment suspensions during the emergency with only partial compensation through Federal Reserve facilities [S3]

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill is ambitious relief legislation with real benefits for households facing eviction, foreclosure, and debt collection during a crisis. Its scale—unlimited monthly payments until an unemployment benchmark is hit—is far larger than anything enacted, and its structural changes to banking (Federal Reserve retail accounts) would be a major transformation rather than a temporary measure. As designed it would need substantial modification to be fiscally or operationally workable, and it never advanced far enough to be refined.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and referred to six House committees but never received a hearing, a committee vote, or a floor vote before the 116th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Representative Maxine Waters introduced the bill on March 23, 2020, in the early weeks of the COVID-19 pandemic [S1, S5]
It was referred to six committees: Financial Services, Ways and Means, Education and Labor, Small Business, Judiciary, and Agriculture [S1, S5]
No further action was taken; the bill received no cosponsors and never advanced to a floor vote before the Congress ended on January 3, 2021 [S4, S5]

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Renters, homeowners, and debtors did not receive the enhanced monthly payments, eviction moratorium, and debt-collection suspension the bill offered. Banks, landlords, and debt collectors avoided the payment suspensions and account mandates. Congress instead enacted smaller stimulus checks ($1,200, then $600) and time-limited eviction and foreclosure protections in separate bills.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Banks, landlords, debt collectors; households got smaller aid

for.name: Maxine Waters
for.role: Representative, California; Chair, House Financial Services Committee
for.what_they_did: Sponsored the bill and introduced it on March 23, 2020 [S1, S5]

against.name: House leadership
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill to six committees without scheduling hearings or a floor vote, and it sat until the Congress ended [S5]

sides.party_line_note: The bill was sponsored by a Democrat and drew zero cosponsors from either party, and the House leadership took no action on it [S4].

industries.note: The bill would require member banks to offer no-fee digital dollar wallets and pay interest on them, and would reimburse smaller banks for costs. Banks would lose some discretion over accounts but gain access to a Federal Reserve credit facility to cover liquidity from suspended loan payments [S3].

The bill bars debt collectors from suing, garnishing wages, repossessing property, or shutting off utilities during the emergency, and blocks them from charging fees or penalty interest on missed payments [S3].

Rent obligations for assisted housing tenants are suspended with federal reimbursement to owners, and eviction filings are barred nationwide; multifamily owners can get mortgage forbearance but must pass relief to tenants [S3].
Servicers must grant broad forbearance requests without documentation but gain access to a Federal Reserve credit facility to cover the cost of advancing payments to investors [S3].
Companies receiving federal aid face a temporary stock buyback ban, disclosure requirements, and potential warrants issued to the government [S2, S3].
